truth.problem: recordPlanRevision appends the journal line, then swallows a failed cursor (commit-marker) write with a stderr log only and still returns the entry as recorded; setExecutionPlan/updateExecutionPlan resolve as success.
truth.impact: When the cursor write fails (disk full, permission, rename error) the appended revision sits past the cursor: ExecutionPlanHistory/renderExecutionPlanChangelog omit it although the write reported success, and the next successful record advances the cursor and silently commits the stale line, so journal and marker disagree and the changelog shows wrong history.

truth.problem: ExecutionPlanHistory's constructor performs synchronous file I/O (reads cursor and journal, parses, may throw) instead of taking loaded entries or exposing a static/async load.
truth.impact: The class cannot be constructed without a real session dir on disk, so tests and callers must stage files; construction can throw I/O errors and blocks the event loop.

truth.problem: describeChange dispatches on the PlanTransition kind discriminant with a five-branch if/else-if chain, while the same module family uses Record<Status, ...> lookup maps for this kind of dispatch (SNAPSHOT_STATUS_RANK in execution-plan.ts, STATUS_LABEL in flow/check-ac.ts).
truth.impact: Adding a transition kind needs another branch and the final bare else silently absorbs any new kind as 'moved'; a Record<PlanTransition['kind'], ...> map would be exhaustiveness-checked.

truth.problem: diffExecutionPlans writes its result into a caller-supplied array (output argument) and returns void instead of returning the transitions.
truth.impact: Callers must pre-allocate and know the array is mutated; reusing a non-empty array silently mixes results; the function cannot be used in an expression.

truth.problem: The same entity is named 'transition' (PlanTransition, entry.transitions, the diff output) and 'change' (describeChange, changesFor, the `change` parameters) within the diff.
truth.impact: Readers must work out that changes and transitions are the same records; searching for one name misses the other.

truth.problem: parseEntry throws a generic "Invalid entry" with no journal path, line number, or failing field (contrast the cursor error and ExecutionPlanValidationError, which carry context).
truth.impact: A corrupt plan-history.jsonl makes the changelog fail with a message that does not say which file or line to fix.

decoys.problem: Catch block around JSON.parse of the cursor file that replaces the parse error with a new Error.
decoys.impact: None: the failure still propagates, with the original error as cause and the file path in the message.
decoys.quote: throw new Error(`plan history cursor ${planHistoryCursorPath(dir)} is not valid JSON`, { cause: error });
decoys.why_not_a_defect: The catch does not swallow or hide anything: it rethrows with { cause } preserved, names the offending file, and the comment explains why guessing a revision would be wrong. This is the recommended error-wrapping pattern, not an empty/log-only catch or a generic error.

candidate.problem: The constructor runs `.map(parseEntry)` over every line before `.filter((entry) => entry.revision <= committed)`. Consider a writer that dies partway through `appendFile`, which is exactly the case the cursor doc comment (lines 27-31) says is handled. It leaves a torn last line, so `JSON.parse` in `parseEntry` throws a bare SyntaxError, and the uncommitted line is never filtered out. The comment says such a line "is never shown as history", which overstates what the code does: it does not hide the line, it makes the whole history unreadable. `parseEntry`'s own error, `new Error("Invalid entry")`, names neither the file nor the line nor the revision, and no `cause` is attached. Compare `readCursor` a few lines up, which names the path for the same reason.
candidate.impact: Once a torn or uncommitted line is in `plan-history.jsonl`, every `new ExecutionPlanHistory(dir)` throws, and so does every `renderExecutionPlanChangelog(dir, ...)` that depends on it. The operator gets "Invalid entry" or a JSON SyntaxError with no file path, so they cannot tell which file to repair. Fix: filter or skip lines above the cursor before parsing them, and make the parse error carry `planHistoryPath(dir)` and the line number, with `{ cause }`.

candidate.problem: `recordPlanRevision` is awaited inside the lock right after `plan.json` has been committed by `writeFileAtomic`. If `appendFile` rejects (ENOSPC, EACCES, a read-only session dir), `writePlan` throws even though the plan write already succeeded. The failure reported belongs to the journal, a secondary side effect, but the caller reads it as a failed plan write. `notify(dir, plan)` is then skipped. The policy is also inconsistent: a cursor-write failure in the same function is swallowed and only logged (G3), while a journal-append failure is fatal to the primary write.
candidate.impact: Trigger: any `appendFile` failure in `setExecutionPlan` or `updateExecutionPlan`. Outcome: the caller is told the plan write failed and subscribers are not notified, yet `plan.json` already holds the new revision. A caller that retries with the same `expectedRevision` then gets `ExecutionPlanConflictError`. Fix: decide one failure policy for the journal and apply it to both writes. Either treat it as best effort, with an explained catch, or make it part of the commit and say so.

candidate.problem: If the cursor write fails, the catch only writes to stderr and then `recordPlanRevision` returns the entry as if it had been journaled. No comment says why this fallback is correct (error-handling.mdc Rule 3). By the module's own commit-marker design, an entry above the cursor is uncommitted, so the revision that was just written is invisible to readers. Nothing the caller can see marks it as degraded.
candidate.impact: Caller: `writePlan`, and through it `renderExecutionPlanChangelog`. Outcome: after a failed cursor write, the changelog leaves out the latest revision and the `latest` header (`history.latestRevision`) is one revision behind, while the write is reported as a success. The revision only shows up if a later write advances the cursor. If it is the last write of the session, it never does. Fix: propagate the error, or return a degraded marker that the caller can see.

candidate.problem: `diffExecutionPlans` takes an output argument: it pushes into a caller-supplied `out: PlanTransition[]` and returns `void`, where it could simply return the array. Neither call site needs to accumulate across calls. Both `recordPlanRevision` and the test allocate an empty array just to pass it in.
candidate.impact: Every caller pays for boilerplate (`const out = []; diff(a, b, out);`). The signature also invites accidental reuse of a non-empty array, which would mix two diffs together. Returning `PlanTransition[]` removes both costs.

candidate.problem: The `ExecutionPlanHistory` constructor does synchronous file I/O and parsing: it reads the cursor file and the journal with `readFileSync` and parses every line. This breaks solid-principles.mdc Iron Law 2, "A constructor performs no I/O". The class mixes loading the journal from disk with querying the loaded entries (`since`, `changesFor`, `latestRevision`).
candidate.impact: The query methods cannot be unit-tested without a real directory on disk. Corrupt-file errors surface from `new` (the test has to assert that `() => new ExecutionPlanHistory(dir)` throws). Fix: a static or free loader such as `loadExecutionPlanHistory(dir)` that reads the files and passes the parsed entries to a constructor that only assigns.

candidate.problem: `describeChange` handles the last case of the `PlanTransition` union with a bare `else` that implicitly means `reordered`, with no exhaustiveness check (`switch` plus a `never` default). If a sixth `kind` is added to the union, the compiler will not flag this function, and the new kind will be rendered through the `moved ${from + 1} -> ${to + 1}` branch.
candidate.impact: This is a future-maintenance risk only: it does not reach any current path. A `switch (change.kind)` with an `assertNever` default would turn that future mistake into a compile error.
